function: Prediction of moving aerial eavesdroppers' positions and thus BS-UAV channels with LSTM and meta-learner LSTM, to enable predictive secure ISAC beamforming (p. 6-8).
system: ISAC downlink: full-duplex BS with L=36 UPA antennas, N=8 users, U=3 UAV eavesdroppers, 1.2x1.2 km area, wavelength 0.01 m (about 30 GHz); no RIS (p. 3, 9).
method: LSTM sequence predictor trained offline (supervised, MSE) and meta-learning LSTM (MAML-style, few-shot fine-tuning steps) for new trajectories; beamforming by SCA and zero forcing, not learned (p. 6-8).
data_channel: Simulated UAV trajectories (constant-acceleration model, 1.5 s slots) and single-path steering-vector channel with path-loss exponent 2.2; custom simulator, no dataset (p. 4, 9).
test_conditions: LSTM trained on trajectories with the same velocity/acceleration as the test (same task) or on a meta dataset of different velocities/accelerations, then fine-tuned with F steps (p. 11).
baselines: Perfect-eavesdropper-channel bound, unsecure communication, different estimation periods T; exhaustive search and heuristic for ML estimation; LSTM trained on same task. No Kalman or other learned predictor compared (p. 9-11).
metrics: Time-average sum secrecy rate; MSE and CRLB of angle and channel-gain estimates; predicted-trajectory plot against the true trajectory (p. 9-11).
complexity: Order of complexity: estimation O(kmax(U^3+U δ)), LSTM O(ω) per step with ω weights, beamforming O(L^3.5 (N+U)^3.5 kmax) (p. 9).
q1_support: p. 9: "the devices are randomly placed within a square area of 1.2 × 1.2 km2"; the channel is a custom single-path steering-vector model with path-loss exponent 2.2 (p. 3-4, Table II on p. 9). No 3GPP model, DeepMIMO, or measured data.
q2_support: p. 3: "fast adaptation to predict different trajectories with a few fine-tuning steps"; p. 11: "the meta-learner LSTM provides a good prediction performance that is improved as the fine-tuning steps F increases" (meta dataset of different velocities and accelerations, Fig. 10).
q3_support: p. 9: "Perfect eavesdropper channel, which represents a hypothetical benchmark" and p. 10: "Unsecure communication scenario" are the references; p. 11 (Fig. 10) compares only the same-task LSTM and meta-LSTM variants. No Kalman filter (named only in p. 2) or other earlier learned predictor is compared.
q4_support: p. 9: "the overall complexity of the LSTM per time step is O(ω), where ω is the number of weights"; the same page gives the overall per-step order O(kmax(U^3+U δ)+L^3.5(N+U)^3.5 kmax+ω).
q5_support: p. 9: "the devices are randomly placed within a square area of 1.2 × 1.2 km2": simulated scenario. No code or data link, and no public dataset, appears in the 12 pages.
notes: PDF page 1 holds the title 'Predictive Beamforming Approach for Secure Integrated Sensing and Communication With Multiple Aerial Eavesdroppers' and DOI 10.1109/TCOMM.2025.3545678. Included with area 2: the only learned parts are the LSTM and meta-learner LSTM that predict the eavesdroppers' positions and thus their channels (p. 6); the ML estimation and the SCA and ZF beamforming are classical. Borderline function: the LSTM output is the UAV position, mapped to the channel by Eq. (2); if the reviewer reads it as target tracking, exclude as localization. The LSTM architecture, dataset size, and training settings are not given. q2 rests on the meta-learning adaptation to new trajectories (Fig. 10, qualitative only).
